# US Households Spend $295 a Month on Utilities


Written by


[Maggie Gunara](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/maggie-gunara/)


Edited by


[Becca Stanek](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/becca-stanek/)


Updated Nov 02, 2026


Content was accurate at the time of publication.


We are committed to providing accurate content that helps you make informed money decisions. Our partners have not commissioned or endorsed this content. Read oureditorial guidelines here .


Utility bills are one of the household expenses you can’t opt out of. Whether it’s a heat wave or a cold snap, the lights, water and climate control likely have to keep running. But how much you’re paying for them depends enormously on where you live.


A LendingTree analysis of the 50 largest U.S. metros found that the typical American household pays $294.66 a month for utilities. What that overall average hides, however, is wide gaps in utility costs between metros, as well as a mixed year-over-year picture and a long-term run of price increases that’s outpaced inflation.


Here’s what the data shows, plus a look at how to prioritize bills when you’re dealing with[debt](https://www.lendingtree.com/debt-consolidation/debt-consolidation-programs/) .


Key findings


- **American households pay an average of $294.66 a month in utility costs.** Among households that pay each bill, electricity is the largest average monthly expense at $198.08, well ahead of gas at $113.74. Water and other home heating fuel follow at $106.47 and $60.01, respectively.
- **Fresno, Calif., has the highest average utility bill among the 50 largest metros.** At $409.63 a month, Fresno’s average is $114.97 higher than the U.S. average. Boston ($370.59) and Birmingham, Ala. ($364.03), follow.
- **Denver, Minneapolis and Jacksonville, Fla., have the lowest average utility costs among the 50 largest metros.** Denver households pay $238.19 a month on average, followed by Minneapolis ($249.24) and Jacksonville ($252.49).
- **In Fresno, utility costs also take the biggest bite out of income.** Average monthly utility costs in Fresno equal 6.6% of the metro’s median monthly household income — the highest share among the 50 largest metros. Birmingham and Memphis, Tenn., follow at 5.8% and 5.7%, respectively.
- **Nationwide, average utility costs dipped slightly in 2024, down $1.68 a month, or 0.6%, from 2023.** But that decline wasn’t universal: Costs rose in 24 of the 50 largest metros. San Jose, Calif., had the largest increase at 8.7%, followed by Birmingham and Charlotte, N.C., both at 7.7%.
- **Electricity and gas prices have outpaced overall inflation since 2016.** From 2016 to 2025, utility (piped) gas prices rose 59.1%, and electricity prices increased 41.1%. Overall consumer prices rose 34.1% over the same period.


## The typical U.S. household pays $295 a month for utilities


Across the country, the average household spends $294.66 a month on utilities. Electricity is the heavyweight: Among households that pay for each service, electricity averages $198.08 a month, well above gas at $113.74. The average water bill comes in at $106.47, while other home heating fuel, such as oil, wood or kerosene, averages $60.01.


Part of the reason that electricity bills in particular run so high is that it’s so hard to cut back on usage.


“Electricity touches nearly every part of our lives at home, and that makes the bill hard to shrink,” says Matt Schulz, LendingTree’s chief consumer finance analyst and author of “Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More: How to Take Control of Your Financial Life.”


“People can turn off lights or adjust the thermostat, but you can’t just cancel your electricity bill like a streaming service. The other challenge is that even when households use less electricity, higher rates can eat into those savings.”


The aforementioned national figures also mask big differences by location. Boston, for instance, has the highest average gas bill at $176.79 — significantly above the national average. Meanwhile, San Jose, Calif., leads for water at $101.47, and New York tops the list for other home heating fuel at $198.91.


## Fresno, Calif., residents pay the most of any large metro


Fresno, Calif., has the highest utility bills among the 50 largest metros, with residents there paying an average of $409.63 a month. That’s $114.97 more than the national average. Boston ($370.59) and Birmingham, Ala. ($364.03), round out the top three.


Electricity is a major driver of the high bills in Fresno. Among households that pay each bill, the average electric bill there is $306.23 a month — the highest of any metro.


In addition, Schulz says these metros are typically more reliant on utilities than others.


“Utility costs are where climate, housing and local rates all collide,” Schulz says. “In a place like Fresno, with long, hot summers, air conditioning can work overtime for months. If your home is older, larger or poorly insulated, the air conditioner has to work just that much harder. Add in local electricity, gas, water and sewer rates, and bills can climb quickly.”


At the other end of the spectrum, Denver has the lowest average utility bill among the 50 largest metros, at $238.19 a month. Minneapolis follows at $249.24, and Jacksonville, Fla., is close behind at $252.49. Notably, a household in Denver pays about $171 less per month than one in Fresno — a gap of more than $2,000 a year.

## In Fresno, utilities also eat up the biggest share of income


In Fresno, utility costs also take the biggest bite out of income. Average monthly utility costs there equal 6.6% of the metro’s median monthly household income — the highest share among the 50 largest metros. Birmingham and Memphis, Tenn., follow at 5.8% and 5.7%, respectively.


These percentages are important information when understanding the real impact of utility bills.


“The dollar amount tells you how big the bill is, but the share of income tells you how painful it is,” Schulz says. “Two households can face the same utility bill and experience it completely differently depending on what they earn. When utilities take up as much of the typical monthly household income as they do in Fresno, it leaves less cash for paying other essential bills as well as working toward longer-term financial goals. That’s a scary spot to be in, but that’s exactly where many Americans find themselves today.”


On the other end of the list, utility costs consume the smallest share of income in metros where incomes are among the highest. San Jose has the lowest percentage, with utilities accounting for just 2.5% of median monthly income. Denver and the District of Columbia follow, at 2.6% each.

## Bills fell slightly in 2024, but not everywhere


Nationally, average utility costs declined in 2024, falling $1.68 a month, or 0.6%, from 2023. That relief wasn’t universal, though, as costs climbed in 24 of the 50 largest metros. San Jose saw the steepest jump at 8.7%, increasing by $27.70 from $319.83 to $347.53.


That’s followed by Birmingham and Charlotte, N.C., which both rose 7.7%.


“National averages can mask enormous differences from one city to another,” Schulz says. “Even as costs tick down nationwide, families in many metros are still paying more. That’s because our utility bills are shaped by local factors like weather, rate changes, energy prices and more. That means that the challenges people face in San Jose can be very different from what people are facing in Fresno, Denver or Minneapolis.”


Meanwhile, costs fell 10.6% in Denver — the only metro to see a double-digit decrease. Minneapolis (9.6%) and Indianapolis (8.4%) followed.

## Electricity and gas prices have outrun inflation for nearly a decade


Over the long haul, energy costs have grown faster than the cost of living. From 2016 to 2025, utility (piped) gas prices jumped 59.1% and electricity prices rose 41.1%. Over the same period, overall consumer prices increased 34.1%.

Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).


This spells bad news for people’s budgets.


“When electricity and gas prices rise faster than overall inflation, they take a bigger bite out of people’s budgets,” Schulz says. “That’s especially difficult for families whose paychecks haven’t kept up, because there may not be much left to cut. You can delay a vacation or dine out less, but you still need to heat or cool your home. Over time, those higher bills shrink people’s already small financial margin for error down to nearly zero.”


## Take control of rising utility bills


Higher utility costs can put extra pressure on a[household budget](https://www.lendingtree.com/personal/budget-to-pay-off-debt/) , but small changes can help. We offer the following advice:


- **Start with the easy wins.** “Adjust the thermostat a few degrees, seal up drafty windows and unplug devices that you’re not using, for example,” Schulz says. “Those things may not sound like much, but they can add up.”
- **Consider a level-payment plan if available.** “Under these plans, you typically pay a monthly bill that’s an average of the past 12 months of payments,” he says. “They won’t reduce what you owe overall, but they can make your bills more predictable, which can be helpful.”
- **Don’t be afraid to ask for help.** “You probably have more options than you think you do, as many utility providers will have customer assistance programs designed to help people struggling with short-term financial woes,” he says. “The sooner you pursue them, the better, though. It’s easier to have those conversations in anticipation of potentially missing a payment than after you’ve already missed several.”


## Methodology


LendingTree analysts used U.S. Census Bureau 2024 American Community Survey one-year microdata obtained through IPUMS to estimate utility costs across the 50 largest U.S. metros.


For each utility — electricity, gas, water and other home heating fuel — we calculated weighted average annual costs among households that paid that bill separately, then divided the result by 12 to calculate the average monthly bill for each utility type. Households whose costs were included in rent or condo fees, or that reported no charge or no use, were excluded from each utility’s calculation.


We also calculated the average monthly utility cost per household by adding each household’s separately paid utility costs across all four categories, then averaging those totals. Utilities where households didn’t pay separately were counted as $0, so this measure excludes utility costs bundled into rent or condo fees.


The analysis includes occupied housing units only and excludes vacant units and group quarters.


The results were used to calculate the following by metro:


- Average monthly utility costs per household in 2024
- Change in average monthly utility costs per household from 2023 to 2024
- Average monthly utility costs as a share of median monthly household income in 2024


Researchers also analyzed the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) to determine how utility prices changed between 2016 and 2025.

**Home Equity Loans and Home Equity Lines of Credit** are both secured by your home and generally require available equity in the property. If you become delinquent on your mortgage or home equity payments, you could lose your home through foreclosure. Before selecting either product, carefully consider your ability to repay the additional debt and review the interest rates, points, fees, repayment terms, and other conditions associated with the loan. Qualification depends on lender underwriting criteria, available home equity, and your ability to repay, and lenders may review factors such as your credit score, credit history, employment history, debt, income, and overall financial profile. Some lenders may also require that you maintain an account with them or meet minimum equity requirements. Generally, home equity loans are not available for homes currently listed for sale. Homes previously listed for sale may be required to remain off the market for at least 90 days prior to applying for a home equity loan or HELOC. Consumers should consult with a financial advisor or other professional before making financial decisions.


**Home Equity Loans** generally provide borrowers with a lump-sum loan amount secured by the equity in their home and typically feature a fixed interest rate and consistent monthly payments over the repayment term. Interest paid on a Home Equity Loan may be tax deductible; however, consumers should consult with a financial advisor or tax professional regarding their individual circumstances. Consumers should also ask lenders about any applicable prepayment penalties.


**Home Equity Lines of Credit (HELOC)** are revolving lines of credit secured by the equity in your home that allow borrowers to access funds during a defined draw period, such as 10 years. During the draw period, borrowers may draw funds as needed, repay amounts owed, and draw additional funds again, similar to the use of a credit card. HELOCs may be a suitable option for borrowers who do not need all available funds at one time. HELOCs generally have variable interest rates tied to a predefined index, such as the U.S. Prime Rate, which means monthly payment amounts may fluctuate over time. Repayment terms vary by lender and may include both a draw period and a repayment period, such as a 30-year term that includes a 10-year draw period. For more information, see[http://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/201204_CFPB_HELOC-brochure.pdf](http://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/201204_CFPB_HELOC-brochure.pdf) .
